# Background

Cemetery records provide individual birth and death dates that can be used to describe lifespan among people represented in a burial ground. These records are a non-random sample: cemetery access, preservation of markers, migration, family burial practices, and the choice of graves to record may all affect which people appear in the dataset. The analyses below therefore describe the collected sample and should not be treated as direct estimates of lifespan for an entire town or historical population.

# Hypotheses

I hypothesized that women would have a greater lifespan than men in this sample because men are typically drafted in wars and also display more reckless behavior in their youth.

# Methods

## Field Site and Sampling

- **Location:** We went to Sunset Hill Cemetery in Valdosta, Georgia next to Valdosta State University's campus on Thursday October 8th. We stayed near the entrance of the cemetery and split up by the gate. 
- **Date & Time of Day:** On October 8th we started our investigation in the cemetary around 2:30 pm and we finished around 4:30 pm. The weather was clear and suitable for our field work.
- **Part of Cemetery Sampled:** I sampled the South East section of the cemetary in rows.
- **Grave Selection:** Sampling was based on how legible the markings of each grave was. Besides that grave selection was random and done by completeing rows.
- **Process of Data Collection for Nearby Graves & Family Plots:** Neighboring graves such as family plots were recorded. Few family plots were found in my section and mainly comprised of married couples. So, there was no overabundance of the same families in my sample.

## Recorded information and variable definitions

- **Information Collected from Each Marker:** Data collected from each marker included name, birth date, date death, sex, marriage status, and veteran status. 
- **Calculation of Lifespan:** Lifespan was calculated from subtracting birth year from the death year. Partial dates were not recorded.
- **Determination of Maritial Status:** Maritial Status was determined through joint graves with the same last names or writing containing "Husband and Wife."
- **Determination of Military Service:** [Describe explicit evidence such as service branch, rank, unit, or veteran symbols. Explain how uncertain cases were coded.] Evidence of military service was only recorded if ranks were etched on the grave.
- **Determination of Sex or Gender:** Sex was determined through explicit titles like wife, mother, sister, etc. being used. If no title was found then an inference was made based on naming conventions.
- **Handling of Missing, Lllegible, or Ambiguous Records:** Any name or date that was ambigious for our records was excluded.

## Dataset and analysis

- **Total Records Collected:** 32 records were collected by me.
- **Amount of Records Included in the Final Analysis:** 30 records were included in the final analysis. 2 were excluded due to no death dates or having a missing family name.
- **Aggregation of Records with Class Dataset:** Yes, my records were aggregated to the class dataset. Our professor, Dr. Hendrickson, sorted and got rid of any duplicates found in this dataset. 
- **Summaries or Plots Produced:** [Describe group summaries and empirical survivorship curves, including how categories were defined.] Our sample shows relationships between survivorship and birth period, sex, martial status, and military status. A positive relationship exsists between each category and shows a correlation in both factors. 
- **Limitations of the Sample:** Limitations of the sample include damage to graves reducing sample size, imcomplete dates, uneven documentation, possible inaccuracies in sex due to naming conventions, and not being able to document military service on graves that don't mention service.

The summary table in @fig-sex shows substantial differences in recorded lifespan by sex in this sample. Males had a mean lifespan of 62.2 years (SD = 23; n = 410), compared with 71.1 years (SD = 23.0; n = 342) for females. These relatively small subgroup sizes make the values descriptive; they do not support broad conclusions about sex. More data would be needed to draw a conclusion.*

![Summary of lifespan by sex.](lifespan_tables/sex.png){#fig-summary width=90% fig-pos="t" fig-env="figure*"}

*The sex-specific survivorship curves in @fig-sex show a different pattern: the plotted means are 62.2 years for males and 71.1 years for females. The female curve remains higher through much of the earlier and middle lifespan, while the male curve reaches the 50% survival point later. The curves are close and change relative position, so the figure suggests that the sex difference depends on which part of the lifespan distribution is considered. The median markers indicate where each group’s observed curve reaches 50% surviving; they are distinct from the mean values shown in the legend.*

![Survivorship curves by sex. The y-axis shows the percentage of the cemetery sample surviving to each lifespan. Dotted vertical lines mark the median lifespan for each sex, where the curve reaches 50%.](survivorship_curves/survivorship_by_sex.png){#fig-sex width=70% fig-pos="t" fig-env="figure*"}

*The within-sex comparisons in @fig-married show higher plotted mean lifespans for married than unmarried individuals in both panels. For males, the plotted means are 64.3 years for married individuals and 55.4 years for unmarried individuals. For females, they are 64.3 and 46.3 years, respectively. The curves also place the 50% survival point later for the married groups. These are descriptive differences and should not be interpreted as evidence that marriage caused longer lifespan; other factors and the sizes and composition of the groups could contribute.*

![Survivorship by marital status, with separate male and female panels. Dotted vertical lines mark the median lifespan for each marital-status group, where the curve reaches 50%.](survivorship_curves/survivorship_married_by_sex_combined.png){#fig-married width=70% fig-pos="t" fig-env="figure*"}

# Discussion

**Sex and lifespan.** Research on sex differences in longevity points to a combination of biological, behavioral, and social influences rather than a single explanation. Austad and Fischer review evidence on sex differences in lifespan and aging across species, including humans [@austadSexDifferencesLifespan2016]. In this cemetery sample, the observed female and male curves [describe the pattern] and [support / do not support] the prediction that [state your hypothesis]. The result should be interpreted in the context of this cemetery’s birth cohorts and sampling process; it is not by itself an estimate of a general sex difference in lifespan.

**Marital status and social relationships.** Marriage can correlate with social support, health behaviors, household resources, and social integration, but people’s health can also influence whether they marry or remain married. A large meta-analysis found associations between unmarried status and mortality, with some associations differing by sex [@wangSexDifferencesAssociation2020]; a broader meta-analysis linked social relationships with mortality risk [@holt-lunstadSocialRelationshipsMortality2010]. In this dataset, the comparison of married and not-married records among [men / women / both] showed [describe results]. These cemetery records do not measure relationship quality, social contact, or the timing and duration of marriage, so marital status should be treated as an imperfect indicator rather than a direct measure of socialization or a cause of longevity.

**Historical changes in lifespan and childhood survival.** Life expectancy at birth is strongly affected by deaths in infancy and childhood, so a low historical average does not mean that every adult died young. Improvements in clean water and sanitation contributed substantially to mortality declines in the United States during the twentieth century, especially for infants and children [@cutlerRolePublicHealth2005]. The birth-period pattern in this sample [describe results] may be consistent with changing survival conditions, but birth year alone cannot identify which changes mattered. Vaccination, nutrition, medical care, living conditions, and the incomplete representation of people in cemetery records may also contribute to differences across cohorts.
